name: Mapping Financial AI to the Rules
title: Mapping Financial AI to the Rules
answer: This page maps where financial AI systems intersect with formal rules, including prudential regulation, securities law, anti-money laundering requirements, data protection, and contractual obligations. It covers the inventory of company pages, merger and acquisition filings, listed AI-related instruments, compliance and regulation pages, active AI lawsuits, AI tools, and glossary terms that the site tracks. The aim is to show which rules apply to which systems, not to advise on compliance. It includes both deployed systems and those in procurement or pilot.

sections.body: This page maps where financial AI systems intersect with formal rules, including prudential regulation, securities law, anti-money laundering requirements, data protection, and contractual obligations. It covers the inventory of company pages, merger and acquisition filings, listed AI-related instruments, compliance and regulation pages, active AI lawsuits, AI tools, and glossary terms that the site tracks. The aim is to show which rules apply to which systems, not to advise on compliance. It includes both deployed systems and those in procurement or pilot.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The mapping runs on the site's structured database of 432 company pages, 352 merger and acquisition filings, 117 listed AI-related instruments, 210 compliance and regulation pages, 142 active AI lawsuits, 732 AI tools, and 674 glossary terms. Each record is tagged by jurisdiction, rule type, and financial function. The infrastructure is a document and metadata store with cross-references, not a live trading or risk engine. Updates come from regulatory publications, court dockets, and company disclosures.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by analysts who read primary sources and assign each AI system or tool to the rules that govern its use. They classify by financial activity, such as credit underwriting, fraud detection, or portfolio management, and by the legal basis, such as a regulation, a contract term, or a supervisory expectation. Where a rule is ambiguous, the page records the open question rather than resolving it. The mapping is reviewed when a new filing, lawsuit, or regulatory notice appears.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights, risk, and provenance are recorded for each mapping entry. The page notes who issued a rule, which authority enforces it, and what rights a customer, employee, or counterparty may have under it. It also flags where a financial AI system creates a new risk, such as unexplained denial of credit or leakage of personal data, and links to the relevant lawsuit or enforcement action. Provenance is kept by citing the source document for every rule-to-system link, so a reader can trace the basis of the mapping.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The mapping is moving toward automated extraction from regulatory texts and court filings, but human review remains the control. As more AI-specific financial rules are proposed, the page will add new rule types and cross-border comparisons. The site's counts of company pages, lawsuits, and tools will grow, and the mapping will show which rules are gaining enforcement attention. The direction is a living index of financial AI obligations, not a static list.
